metadata.note: Passenger rail to Adams, Massachusetts, in three eras. The Pittsfield and North Adams Railroad was incorporated March 3 1842 to carry the Housatonic Railroad north toward Vermont and opened December 1 1846, 18.539 miles from North Adams Junction in Pittsfield up the Hoosic valley to North Adams, with stops at Coltsville, Berkshire, Farnams, Cheshire, Cheshire Harbor, Maple Grove, Adams, Renfrew and Zylonite. The Western Railroad of Massachusetts bought it before construction was even finished; it became the Boston and Albany's North Adams Branch in 1870, and the New York Central took control of the B&A in 1900. Its named train was the Berkshire Hills Express, New York to North Adams, 175.5 miles by the Central's Harlem Line to Chatham, the B&A east to Pittsfield and then north up this branch -- Berkshires resort traffic and Williams College students. It ran 1919 to 1934, unnamed successors followed, by 1950 the service was a Chatham-North Adams shuttle requiring transfers, and scheduled passenger service ended in 1953. Separately, the Hoosac Valley Street Railway opened between Adams and North Adams in 1886 and electrified in 1889; absorbed into the Berkshire Street Railway, it carried passengers until that whole system shut down on November 12 1932. The branch was abandoned in 1990 and the Pittsfield-to-Adams half became the Ashuwillticook Rail Trail, but the Adams-North Adams track survived -- and since 2016 the Berkshire Scenic Railway Museum has run the Hoosac Valley Service over it, so Adams has passenger trains again. The 1889 station is a sports bar and restaurant.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkshire_Hills_Express -- New York Central, 1919-1934, New York to North Adams, 175.5 miles via the Harlem Line to Chatham then the B&A to Pittsfield and the North Adams branch; served Adams; resort and Williams College traffic; unnamed successor service to 1953; by 1950 a Chatham-North Adams shuttle.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adams_station_(New_York_Central_Railroad) -- Adams was the town's principal station on the B&A North Adams Branch; station dated 1889 (the article's own text says 1899 -- see not_yet_sourced); now a sports bar and restaurant; right-of-way became the Ashuwillticook Rail Trail.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkshire_Street_Railway -- the Hoosac Valley Street Railway began operating between Adams and North Adams in 1886 and was electrified in 1889 (550 V DC overhead); absorbed into the Berkshire Street Railway; all streetcar service ended November 12 1932.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkshire_Scenic_Railway_Museum and https://www.berkshiretrains.org/ -- 2014 state grant of $200,000 to move excursion operations to the Hoosac Valley; tourist service began 2016; hour-long round trips Adams-North Adams from the platform beside the Adams Visitors Center, weekends Memorial Day to October plus holiday trains Thanksgiving to Christmas; all-volunteer and seasonal.
Geometry: OpenStreetMap relation 1376511 'North Adams Branch' via the OSM API, and MA Route 8 road ways via Overpass, both fetched 2026-08-24.
not_yet_sourced: The trolley alignment is a corridor approximation, not a traced route -- see the geometry_quality on hoosac-valley-street-railway. If a Berkshire Street Railway track map turns up, that feature should be redrawn.

Whether the Hoosac Valley Street Railway ran beyond Adams to the south (toward Cheshire and Pittsfield) as part of the wider Berkshire Street Railway network is not established here; only the documented Adams-North Adams line is drawn.
SOURCE CONFLICT on the Adams station building: the Wikipedia article's text says built 1899, its infobox says opened 1889. 1889 is used in the notes; nothing in this file depends on it.
Every headway_min in this file is an estimate. No timetable was found for the North Adams Branch in any era, for the trolley, or for the current excursion schedule.

The exact 1953 date for the end of scheduled passenger service comes from the Berkshire Hills Express article's statement that service on the segment ended that year; no month or final-train date was found.

The 1846-1870 feature is a composite: the Pittsfield and North Adams was bought by the Western Railroad of Massachusetts before it opened, so the trains were the Western's from day one. The Western Railroad has no other feature in data/, so rather than invent a colour for it the two names share one feature and one colour, with the ownership stated in the segment note.

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap route relation 1376511 'North Adams Branch' (alt_name 'Pittsfield and North Adams Branch', old_railway_operator=NYC), chained end to end over 47 member ways. 502 points, 29.94 km / 18.60 miles against a documented 18.539 miles -- a 0.3% match, which is the check that the chaining is right. No straight-line approximation anywhere. The corridor survives in two forms and the trace follows both: Pittsfield to Adams is now the Ashuwillticook Rail Trail (tagged cycleway and abandoned railway), and Adams to North Adams is still track, the Berkshire and Eastern's Adams Industrial Track. This is the original alignment, contemporary with every era drawn on it.

segments.note: Worked as the Boston and Albany's North Adams Branch from 1870. Adams got its own station in 1889 and it was the town's principal stop for the rest of the line's passenger life. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

The New York Central took control of the Boston and Albany in 1900 and this branch got a through train of its own: the Berkshire Hills Express, New York to North Adams, 175.5 miles by the Central's Harlem Line to Chatham, the B&A east to Pittsfield, then north up this branch through Adams. It ran from 1919, carrying Berkshires resort traffic and Williams College students, and the name was dropped in 1934. This feature keeps the Boston and Albany's name and colour through the New York Central era, matching how boston_and_albany_railroad.geojson already treats the same lease. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

Unnamed successor service after the Berkshire Hills Express name was dropped. By 1950 the through train had shrunk to a Chatham-North Adams shuttle requiring transfers, and scheduled passenger service on the branch ended in 1953 -- the last year drawn here. Freight continued for decades under Penn Central, Conrail, the Boston and Maine and Guilford; the line was abandoned in 1990 and the Pittsfield-to-Adams half became the Ashuwillticook Rail Trail, but no passengers rode those years, so none of them are drawn. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.speed_source: estimated: interurban street running with frequent stops; unsourced
properties.geometry_quality: APPROXIMATE, AND THE WEAKEST GEOMETRY IN THIS FILE. Drawn on today's MA Route 8 between Adams and North Adams -- 216 points, 8.18 km / 5.08 miles -- because no source found gives the Hoosac Valley Street Railway's street-by-street alignment. Route 8 is the valley's through road and the corridor the interurban followed, but part of the drawn line runs on the Curran Memorial Highway, a modern bypass that did not exist in the streetcar era; an attempt to route it entirely on older streets failed for lack of a continuous named-street path. Treat the corridor as right and the exact alignment as unverified. Note this is a DIFFERENT alignment from the railroad features in this file: the trolley ran in the street, the Boston and Albany branch on its own right-of-way about half a mile west.

segments.note: The Hoosac Valley Street Railway began operating between Adams and North Adams in 1886, giving the two towns a local service alongside the steam branch. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

Electrified in 1889 on 550 volt DC overhead wire, and later absorbed into the consolidated Berkshire Street Railway system. Streetcar service through Adams ended with the shutdown of the whole Berkshire Street Railway on November 12 1932. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

No approximation.

segments.note: The Berkshire Scenic Railway Museum won a $200,000 state grant in 2014 to move its excursion operation to the Hoosac Valley and started running in 2016, putting passenger trains back into Adams 63 years after the last scheduled one. Hour-long round trips between Adams and North Adams leave from the platform beside the Adams Visitors Center, weekends from Memorial Day into October with holiday trains from Thanksgiving to Christmas. All-volunteer and seasonal, so the headway is a stand-in for an operating day, not a year-round frequency -- estimated, unsourced.
